text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Do it: Add a "safe change" auto-apply layer to the prompt-review engine. It will patch obvious, low-risk improvements without human review—like fixing typos or standardizing formatting—so the team can focus on high-value work. The trade-off is accepting rare false positives where a harmless change might slip through; we mitigate this by limiting the auto-apply to a narrow set of rules and logging every change for audit.

name: Gauge
text: The "safe change" layer risks normalizing sloppy reviews—what’s "obvious" to one person is a judgment call to another. A better alternative is a staged rollout: start with a narrow set of rules (e.g., only trailing whitespace removal) and measure false positives before expanding. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with strict logging and a post-mortem on every change.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do it: Auto-apply only trailing whitespace removal as the first "safe change" rule. It’s mechanical, zero-risk, and catches 80% of trivial formatting noise without changing meaning. The trade-off is delaying broader auto-fixes, but that’s the point—start narrow to prove the layer works before expanding.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: The "trailing whitespace" rule alone won’t stop teams from gaming the system—if reviewers know auto-apply exists, they’ll dump more slop into reviews expecting the bot to clean it up. A better test is to auto-apply *only* changes that preserve the *exact* diff hash of the original review, proving the bot didn’t alter intent. Settle it by running a 2-week blind trial where reviewers can’t see auto-applied changes, then compare error rates.
